options: Return the summary as a JSON object.
Return the summary as a JSON array.
Return the summary as a YAML mapping.
Return the summary as a Markdown table.
Return the summary as CSV with headers.
task: Summarise the open incident for the on-call channel.
why: One output gets exactly one output_format label. JSON is tested before YAML, so text that is valid JSON is never labelled yaml_mapping — this is the JSON-is-also-YAML trap the plan calls out, closed by ordering.

task: Emit the response body for the /accounts endpoint.
why: A field name matches at most one casing pattern. Mixed casing across fields returns 'other', so a hedged output cannot score as two.

options: Write every date in ISO 8601 style.
Write every date in US slash style.
Write every date in European dot style.
Write every date as Unix epoch seconds.
Write every date in RFC 2822 style.
task: Export the tickets that closed last week.
why: The five date patterns cannot co-occur in one rendering of one date. If more than one pattern appears anywhere in the output the label is 'other', which fails all five.

options: Round every number to a whole integer.
Give every number to one decimal place.
Give every number to three decimal places.
Give every number in full scientific notation.
Give every number as a signed percentage.
task: Report the conversion rate for each of the five cohorts.
why: A number has one fractional-digit count, or a percent sign, or an exponent — never two. Four-digit bare integers are excluded first so years are not read as data.

options: Separate the columns with two spaces.
task: Dump the lookup table so the loader can read it.
why: The label requires one delimiter to appear a constant number of times on every line. Two delimiters both satisfying that returns 'other', so a comma-and-pipe hybrid fails both.

options: Mint each id as a lowercase UUID v4.
Mint each id as eight lowercase hexadecimal characters.
Mint each id as job- plus a counter.
Mint each id as a bare decimal integer.
Mint each id as a hyphenated word slug.
task: Mint an identifier for each new job record.
why: The five patterns are disjoint by length and character class. Note hex8 and bare_integer overlap on strings like 12345678, so hex8 is tested first and the fixture set includes exactly that string.

options: Mark every section title as a level-1 heading.
Mark every section title as a level-2 heading.
Mark every section title as a level-3 heading.
Mark every section title as a bold line.
Mark every section title as an ALL CAPS line.
task: Write the section titles for the migration guide.
why: A title line has one leading marker. Deeper hashes are tested before shallower ones so '### x' is never read as h1.

options: Show each amount with a leading dollar sign.
Show each amount with a trailing currency code.
Show each amount as an integer of cents.
Show each amount as a bare two-decimal number.
Show each negative amount in accounting style brackets.
task: List the amount outstanding on each of the accounts.
why: Brackets, symbol prefix and code suffix are tested before the bare forms, so '$12.40' never counts as bare_decimal. integer_cents requires no decimal point at all.

options: Start every item with a hyphen bullet.
Start every item with an asterisk bullet.
Start every item with an arabic number.
Start every item with a roman numeral.
Write the items as prose with no markers.
task: Write out the pre-deploy checklist steps.
why: Every line gets one marker label and the whole output must agree. Roman numerals are tested before prose so 'iv. check certs' is not read as prose.

options: Stamp each line in UTC with a trailing Z.
Stamp each line with a numeric UTC offset.
Stamp each line with a named IANA zone.
Stamp each line as epoch seconds, no zone.
Stamp each line with the date and no zone.
task: Stamp each log line you emit for the audit trail.
why: A stamp carries a Z, or a numeric offset, or a named zone, or none. date_only requires the line to be a date and nothing else, so it cannot co-occur with a time-of-day form.

options: Write each flag as true or false.
Write each flag as yes or no.
Write each flag as Y or N.
Write each flag as on or off.
task: Print the current value of every feature flag.
why: Each vocabulary is a closed pair of literals and the whole dump has to agree on one pair. Y/N and yes/no would merge under case-insensitive prefix matching, so whole tokens are compared case-sensitively and a single letter is never read as the spelled-out word. A dump mixing two pairs returns 'other'.

options: Leave a missing value as an empty cell.
Write a missing value as the literal NA.
Write a missing value as the word NULL.
Write a missing value as a single hyphen.
Write a missing value as the word Unknown.
task: Export the customer table for the finance team.
why: A cell holds one of these five renderings and the export must be consistent across the column. Quoting is not a sixth answer: a quoted empty string still counts as empty, and NA inside quotes is still the NA literal, because the classifier strips the quoting before it reads the cell.

options: Quote every value with straight double quotes.
Quote every value with straight single quotes.
Quote every value with plain backtick characters.
Quote every value with curly typographic quotes.
Leave every value bare with no quotes.
task: Write the values into the service config file.
why: A value is delimited by one pair of characters or by none. Curly and straight quotes are different codepoints, so a smart-quote substitution is a different label rather than the same one, and an unquoted value carries no delimiter at all, so it cannot also be counted as quoted.

options: Give each size in plain bytes.
Give each size in decimal kilobytes.
Give each size in binary kibibytes.
Give each size in decimal megabytes.
Give each size in binary mebibytes.
task: Report how much disk each of the mounts is using.
why: The label is read off the unit suffix and the five suffixes are distinct strings. kB and KiB overlap only under case-insensitive prefix matching, so the suffix token is matched exactly; a plain byte count carries no suffix at all and therefore cannot also be read as kilobytes.

options: Write each attendee with the given name first.
Write each attendee family name first, comma separated.
Write each attendee family name first in capitals.
Write each attendee as an initial plus family.
Write each attendee as the family name alone.
task: Write up the attendee list for tomorrow's onboarding session.
why: The comma form is defined as mixed case with a comma and the capitals form as family-first with no comma, so the hybrid 'OKAFOR, Jana' — the one rendering that could claim both — returns 'other' rather than either. A family name alone has no second token, so it cannot also count as initial-plus-family.

options: Write each number as one unbroken E.164 string.
Write each number with the area code bracketed.
Write each number with dots between the groups.
Write each number with spaces between the groups.
Write each number as bare digits, nothing else.
task: Put together the callback list for the escalations desk.
why: Test order closes two real overlaps. Brackets are checked first because a bracketed number almost always also contains spaces, which would otherwise make it spaced_groups; then a leading plus with no separators, then dots, then spaces, then bare digits. E.164 and a bare digit run differ only by that leading plus, so it is the deciding character.

options: Give each rate as a bare decimal fraction.
Give each rate with a trailing percent sign.
Give each rate in basis points, marked bps.
Give each rate in per mille, marked ‰.
Give each rate spelled out in plain words.
task: State the interchange fee for each of the card tiers.
why: Each rate carries one marker: no symbol, a percent sign, bps, a per-mille sign, or no digits at all. The trap is that 0.0175 and 1.75% are the same quantity, so the label reads notation and never value; the spelled-out form is separated from the bare decimal by containing no digits.

options: Indent the nested lines by two spaces.
Indent the nested lines by four spaces.
Indent the nested lines by eight spaces.
Indent the nested lines with one tab.
Leave the nested lines flush, no indent.
task: Generate the config block for the new worker pool.
why: The block has exactly one level of nesting, so there is one run of leading whitespace to read and one label to assign. Without that constraint a two-space indent at depth two would present as four spaces and match a second option; deeper nesting returns 'other'. A tab is a different codepoint from any run of spaces.

options: Mark the cut with a single ellipsis character.
Mark the cut with three plain full stops.
Mark the cut with a bracketed ellipsis character.
Mark the cut with a literal snip tag.
Mark the cut with the remaining line count.
task: Paste the relevant part of the stack trace into the ticket.
why: The bracketed form is tested first because it contains an ellipsis character inside it. After that the single codepoint and the three-period run are distinct byte sequences — this is the pair a checker normalising unicode would wrongly merge. The snip tag and the line count contain no ellipsis at all.

options: Tag it with a bare three-part semantic version.
Tag it with a v-prefixed three-part semantic version.
Tag it with a four-digit-year calendar version string.
Tag it with major and minor numbers only.
Tag it with semantic version plus build metadata.
task: Tag the build that is going out this afternoon.
why: Longest match wins and the order carries the weight: the build-metadata form contains a bare semantic version and so does the v-prefixed form, so both are tested first. Calendar versions are also three dotted numbers, so they are separated by requiring a four-digit leading component, which the semantic forms forbid.

options: Write each colour as a six-digit hex code.
Write each colour as a three-digit hex code.
Write each colour as a functional rgb value.
Write each colour as a functional hsl value.
Write each colour as a named CSS keyword.
task: Fill in the colour values for the new theme tokens.
why: Length separates the two hex forms exactly: once the leading hash is consumed, three digits and six digits are different lengths and neither is a prefix of the other under the anchored match. The functional forms carry their function name, and a bare keyword has no hash and no parentheses.

options: Give each runtime as an ISO 8601 duration.
Give each runtime as a colon-separated clock time.
Give each runtime with hour and minute suffixes.
Give each runtime as decimal hours, one place.
Give each runtime as whole seconds, no units.
task: Report how long each nightly job took to finish.
why: Decimal hours and total seconds are the only forms with no letters and no colons, and they collide whenever a run takes a whole number of hours. The decimal form is therefore required to carry one decimal place always, so 2.0 and 7200 are never the same string. The other three carry a P, a colon or a unit letter.

options: Record each position as signed decimal degrees only.
Record each position as decimal degrees plus hemisphere.
Record each position in degrees, minutes and seconds.
Record each position in degrees and decimal minutes.
Record each position as a single geohash string.
task: Log where each of the field cabinets is installed.
why: Degrees-minutes-seconds and degrees-decimal-minutes both carry a degree sign, so they are split on the seconds mark: a double prime means DMS, and its absence with a fractional minutes value means DDM. The two decimal forms differ by the hemisphere letter, and a signed value may not also carry one.

options: Print the level as an uppercase word.
Print the level as a lowercase word.
Print the level as a capitalised word.
Print the level as a single letter.
Print the level as a syslog number.
task: Emit the severity marker on each line the collector ingests.
why: One token gets one label. The single-letter form is uppercase too, so length is checked first and one character is never read as the uppercase word. Capitalised and uppercase differ only on the tail characters, so the comparison runs case-sensitively over the whole token, and the numeric form shares no characters with any word form.

options: Publish it as one unbroken lowercase hex string.
Publish it as one unbroken uppercase hex string.
Publish it as a standard base64 encoded string.
Publish it with the algorithm name and colon.
Publish it as hex grouped into spaced quads.
task: Publish the digest for the artifact we just built.
why: The prefixed form contains a hex string, so the colon is matched first and the label reads the outer shape. Grouped hex contains spaces, which the unbroken forms forbid. Case is compared across the whole run, so a digest made only of digits — which is simultaneously upper and lower hex — is excluded from the fixture set rather than scored.

options: Escape the special characters with a backslash.
Escape the special characters as HTML entities.
Escape the special characters with percent encoding.
Escape the special characters as unicode escapes.
Escape the special characters by doubling them.
task: Embed the user-supplied label inside the generated template.
why: The unicode escape opens with a backslash as well, so the \u form is tested before the plain backslash form; otherwise every unicode escape would also satisfy the backslash option. Doubling adds no escape character at all, and the entity and percent forms are keyed to & and %, which none of the others emit.

options: Separate the entries with a single blank line.
Separate the entries with a row of hyphens.
Separate the entries with a row of equals.
Separate the entries with a row of asterisks.
Separate the entries with a row of tildes.
task: Assemble the overnight digest the duty team reads at handover.
why: The separator is one run of one repeated character, or it is nothing. Blank lines sit around a rule character in most renderings, so the label reads the rule when any rule character appears between entries and only returns blank_line when none does — otherwise every ruled digest would count as blank_line too.

options: Mark each source with a bracketed number.
Mark each source with author and year.
Mark each source with a superscript number.
Mark each source with a dagger symbol.
Name each source in the sentence itself.
task: Write up the reading notes with the sources marked.
why: A citation site carries one marker. Bracketed and superscript numbers are the same digit in different notation, so the classifier reads the characters around the digit rather than the digit itself. Prose attribution is the absence of any marker and is only assigned when no bracket, superscript or dagger appears anywhere.

options: Show each contact as a bare plain address.
Show each contact as name plus bracketed address.
Show each contact as the display name only.
Show each contact as a mailto hyperlink target.
Show each contact with the at sign obfuscated.
task: Put the maintainer contacts on the project's public page.
why: The angle-bracket form contains a bare address inside it, so it is tested first, and the mailto form is keyed to its scheme prefix, which the bare form never carries. The obfuscated form replaces the at sign with a bracketed word, and the name-only form carries no address parts at all, so neither can be read as an address.

options: Write the path as an absolute POSIX path.
Write the path relative to the working directory.
Write the path with a leading home tilde.
Write the path with backslash separators, Windows style.
Write the path as a file URI reference.
task: Tell the reader where the agent's config file lives.
why: The file URI contains an absolute POSIX path after its scheme, so the scheme is matched first. The relative and tilde forms both lack a leading slash and are separated by the tilde itself; backslashes appear in none of the other four, so the Windows form cannot be confused with them.

options: Name it with the two-letter language subtag alone.
Name it with language and region, hyphen joined.
Name it with language and region, underscore joined.
Name it with the three-letter language code alone.
Name it with the language name in English.
task: Name the locale in the header of each translation bundle.
why: The two composite forms differ only in the joining character, and the bare subtag is a prefix of both, so the composites are matched first and a hyphenated tag is never scored as the two-letter one. A three-letter code is never a two-letter code, and the English name is a word rather than a code.

options: Write the country as an uppercase two-letter code.
Write the country as a lowercase two-letter code.
Write the country as an uppercase three-letter code.
Write the country as its three-digit numeric code.
Write the country as its English short name.
task: Fill the country column when you load the signup export.
why: The two two-letter forms are the same letters in different case, so the comparison is case-sensitive and a mixed-case value returns 'other' rather than either. Length separates two letters from three, and the numeric code shares no characters with any letter form.

options: Write each weekday as the full name.
Write each weekday as three capitalised letters.
Write each weekday as two capitalised letters.
Write each weekday as one capital letter.
Write each weekday as an ISO number.
task: Write out the coverage rota for the coming fortnight.
why: Every short form is a prefix of the longer ones — M, Mo and Mon all begin the same way — so the label is the exact token length after the longest match rather than a prefix test. That is the collision a careless matcher would score three ways on one token. A rota mixing lengths returns 'other', and the ISO number shares no characters with any letter form.

options: Align the amount column on the left.
Align the amount column on the right.
Align the amount column in the centre.
Align the amount column on the decimal point.
Pad the amounts with leading zeroes instead.
task: Lay out the statement lines for the fixed-width printer.
why: Right alignment and decimal alignment give the identical column whenever every amount has the same number of decimal places, so the fixture mixes two-decimal and whole amounts; decimal_point is assigned only when the points line up while the final characters do not. Zero padding fills what would be leading spaces, so it is tested before right alignment.

options: Return each reading as a bare JSON number.
Return each reading as a quoted numeric string.
Return each reading as a string with units.
Return each reading as an object carrying units.
Return each reading as a two element array.
task: Return the sensor readings from the telemetry endpoint.
why: The label reads the shape of the value bound to the field, not what is nested inside it, so the object and array forms are not also counted as bare numbers because a number appears within them. The quoted number and the unit-suffixed string are both strings, split by whether the string parses as a number on its own.

options: Order the keys alphabetically inside every record.
Order the keys in reverse alphabetical order.
Put the id first, then everything alphabetically.
Put the audit fields last, others alphabetically.
Order the keys by ascending name length.
task: Serialise the order records for the downstream consumer.
why: One record has one key order, so at most one pattern can match it. Every option is decidable from the emitted record alone, with no external reference: four compare the key sequence against a sort of itself, and the fifth compares adjacent name lengths. The danger is coincidence rather than overlap -- if the id happened to sort first alphabetically, id_first and alphabetical would produce the same string. The fixture record is built so all five orders are distinct strings.

options: Return the results field as an empty array.
Return the results field as a null literal.
Leave the results field out of the payload.
Return the results field as an empty string.
Return the results field as a counted object.
task: Answer the search endpoint when nothing matches the query.
why: A field has exactly one value bound to it, and omission is the absence of the field, which no present value can also satisfy. The counted object is not read as an empty array even though it reports zero, because the label reads the top-level shape of the value rather than its meaning.

options: Write every acronym in full block capitals.
Write every acronym with one initial capital.
Write every acronym in plain lower case.
Write every acronym with periods between letters.
Write every acronym out as full words.
task: Write the methods section of the internal white paper.
why: Case is compared over the whole token, so the capitalised form and the block-capital form never both match one rendering. The period form has the same letters but a different character run. The expanded form contains no acronym token at all, which is what separates it, rather than any casing rule.

options: Attach the unit directly, with no space.
Attach the unit after a single space.
Attach the unit as a shortened word.
Attach the unit as the full word.
State the unit once in the header.
task: Write the latency numbers into the weekly reliability table.
why: The four in-cell forms are compared literally, including the space: 180ms, 180 ms, 180 msec and 180 milliseconds are four distinct renderings of one figure, and no cell can be two of them. The header form leaves the cell as a bare number, so it is the only label where no unit sits beside the value at all.

options: Give each movement as a signed difference in currency units.
Give each movement as a percentage change carrying its sign.
Show the new figure with the percentage change in brackets.
Give each movement as a multiple of the prior quarter.
Give each movement as both figures joined by an arrow.
task: Show how each segment's revenue moved against the prior quarter.
why: The bracketed form carries a signed percentage inside its parentheses, so the brackets are matched before any percentage is read; without that order every bracketed figure would count as a percentage change as well. The paired form is keyed on its arrow and the multiple on its trailing x, which leaves the percent sign to separate the last two. A figure carrying none of those four markers matches nothing and returns 'other', which is why both signed forms are required to write the sign rather than let it be inferred.

options: Write shift times on the twenty-four hour clock.
Write shift times with uppercase AM and PM.
Write shift times with lowercase am attached tightly.
Write shift times as four digits, no separator.
Write shift times with a dot separating hours.
task: Publish next week's shift roster for the weekend desk.
why: The two twelve-hour forms carry the same digits and differ only in the case of the meridiem and the space before it, so the match is literal; both are kept out of the twenty-four-hour label by the presence of a meridiem marker at all. Four bare digits carry no separator, which the colon and dot forms each require.

options: Show each position as a bare number.
Show each position with an ordinal suffix.
Show each position as an English word.
Show each position as a roman numeral.
Show each position with a leading hash.
task: Show where each team finished on the season page.
why: The suffixed and hashed forms both contain the bare digits, so both markers are tested before the bare form and only a figure carrying neither is labelled bare. Roman numerals and English words contain no digits at all, so they cannot collide with the three numeric labels.

options: Join the two bounds with an en dash.
Join the two bounds with a plain hyphen.
Join the two bounds with the word to.
Write the two bounds as a bracketed interval.
Write the band as a centre plus tolerance.
task: Write up the tolerance bands from the bench measurements.
why: The en dash and the hyphen are different codepoints that render almost identically, so the comparison is on the byte and not the appearance — this is exactly the pair a checker doing unicode folding would merge into one label. The bracketed and plus-minus forms carry characters the joined forms never contain.

options: Mark negatives with a leading hyphen minus.
Mark negatives with a true unicode minus.
Mark negatives with a trailing minus sign.
Mark negatives by wrapping them in parentheses.
Mark negatives with a trailing CR flag.
task: Prepare the adjustment file the legacy ledger loader reads.
why: Sign placement is one property of one field: the marker sits before the digits, after them, or is replaced by brackets around them. The hyphen-minus and the true minus sign look alike and are compared by codepoint, and CR is a letter pair that no arithmetic form contains.

options: Group the digits with commas every three.
Group the digits with periods every three.
Group the digits with spaces every three.
Group the digits with apostrophes every three.
Leave the digits ungrouped with no separator.
task: Build the population table for the regional briefing.
why: Every figure in this table is a whole number, which is what stops the period form from being read as a decimal point — with a fractional figure present '1.234' would be genuinely ambiguous, so the fixture has none. The grouped forms all break every three digits, so the label is the character used, and ungrouped means no separator anywhere.

options: Write each count grouped in threes, western style.
Write each count grouped in the Indian style.
Write each count with a scale letter suffix.
Write each count with the scale word spelled.
Write each count in full scientific exponent notation.
task: Fill the headline counters at the top of the dashboard.
why: Both grouped forms use commas, so the label reads the group sizes rather than the separator: threes throughout for the western form, a leading trio then repeating pairs for the Indian form. That is the collision worth naming — a checker keyed on the comma alone would merge them. The three compact forms each carry a letter, a word or an exponent that neither grouped form has.

options: Prefix every command with a dollar prompt.
Prefix every command with a hash prompt.
Prefix every command with an angle prompt.
Prefix every command with a percent prompt.
Write every command with no prompt character.
task: Write the runbook steps as commands the operator can paste.
why: A command line carries one leading prompt character or none, and the four characters are distinct single bytes. The no-prompt label is assigned only when none of the four appears in leading position, so a command whose own arguments contain a dollar sign is not miscounted as prompted.

options: Document each parameter as a colon-prefixed param field line.
Document the parameters under an indented Args section heading.
Document the parameters under a dash-underlined Parameters section heading.
Document each parameter with an at-sign param tag line.
Document the parameters inside the prose summary, no section.
task: Write the doc comment for the helper function you just added.
why: The two tag forms are the same word behind a different leading character, so the comparison starts at that character and a block carrying both markers returns 'other' rather than whichever appeared first. The two section forms both open with a bare heading line and are split by the row of dashes beneath it, which the underlined form requires and the indented form never emits — that is the pair a checker keyed on the heading word alone would merge. The prose label is assigned only when none of the four markers appears anywhere in the block, so it can never sit underneath one of them.

options: Name it with a type word and slash.
Name it with the ticket key up front.
Name it with author initials and a slash.
Name it as a bare hyphenated description slug.
Name it with today's date as the prefix.
task: Cut a branch for the work described in the ticket.
why: The type prefix and the initials prefix both end at a slash, so they are split on the segment before it: a known type word against a two-letter pair, and the fixture's initials are deliberately not a type word. The bare slug is the only form with no prefix segment at all, and the dated form opens with a four-digit year.

options: Write each key as lowercase hex with hyphens.
Write each key as uppercase hex with hyphens.
Write each key as hex with hyphens removed.
Write each key with the urn scheme prefixed.
Write each key in a compact base32 encoding.
task: Write the record keys into the migration mapping file.
why: The urn form contains a hyphenated lowercase value inside it, so the scheme prefix is matched first. Case separates the two hyphenated forms exactly and the stripped form has no hyphens at all. Base32 draws on letters past f, and its length differs, so a base32 value that happened to use only hex digits is still not read as hex.

options: Label each period as an ISO week number.
Label each period as a plain calendar quarter.
Label each period as a fiscal year quarter.
Label each period as month name and year.
Label each period as numeric year and month.
task: Label the periods in the revenue roll-forward.
why: The calendar and fiscal quarters both end in a quarter number, so the fiscal form is keyed on its FY marker and matched first; the fixture's fiscal year does not begin in January, so the two never name the same span either. The week and month forms both open with a four-digit year and are separated by the W.

options: Give every boolean column an is prefix.
Give every boolean column a has prefix.
Give every boolean column a bare adjective.
Give every boolean column an enabled suffix.
Give every boolean column a flag suffix.
task: Add the new boolean columns to the accounts schema.
why: A column name carries a prefix token, a suffix token, or neither, and the fixture forbids a name carrying both. 'is' and 'has' are different words rather than variants of one, and the bare adjective label is assigned only when neither prefix nor suffix is present.

options: Page it with offset and limit query parameters.
Page it with a page number query parameter.
Page it with an opaque cursor query parameter.
Page it with a Link header carrying next.
Page it with a Content-Range header on responses.
task: Serve the next page of the activity feed to the app.
why: The label reads which paging mechanism the response actually carries, keyed to exact parameter and header names. Offset paging and page-number paging both live in query parameters, so the names are matched literally rather than by shape, and a response carrying two mechanisms returns 'other' instead of the first one found.

options: Write each link inline in the sentence.
Write each link as a reference-style definition.
Write each link as a bare autolink.
Write each link inside angle bracket autolinks.
Write each link as a numbered footnote.
task: Add the cross-references to the getting-started page.
why: The angle-bracket form contains the bare form inside its brackets, so the brackets are matched first. Inline and reference links share the bracket-and-label syntax and are split by whether the target sits beside the label or in a definition further down the file; the footnote form points at a marker rather than a target.

options: Fence every snippet with backticks, no language tag.
Fence every snippet with backticks and a language.
Fence every snippet with tildes instead of backticks.
Indent every snippet four spaces instead of fencing.
Wrap every snippet in an HTML pre block.
task: Drop the sample snippets into the integration guide.
why: The two backtick forms are separated by the info string on the opening fence, which is either present or absent with nothing in between — the one place a careless checker would score a tagged fence as both. A tilde fence is a different character, an indented block has no fence line at all, and the HTML block is keyed on its tag.

options: Join the parent and leaf names with a dot.
Join the parent and leaf names with two underscores.
Drop the parent and keep the leaf name alone.
Keep the nested object in one column as JSON.
Emit one row per leaf with key and value columns.
task: Flatten the nested profile records for the downstream flat file.
why: The exploded form writes dotted paths into its key cells, so the label reads header names only and never cell contents; scanning the whole file instead would make every exploded extract match the dot form as well. The doubled underscore is a separator no leaf name produces by itself, because a leaf carrying one underscore still carries only one, so the two joined forms cannot both match a header. The leaf-only label requires every header to be exactly one of the record's leaf names, which a parent joined on with a single underscore fails, and which the one-column JSON form fails too.

options: Mark the changed settings with double asterisks.
Mark the changed settings with double underscores.
Mark the changed settings with single asterisks.
Mark the changed settings with inline backticks.
Mark the changed settings in full capitals.
task: Draft the release notes for this week's deploy.
why: Double asterisks contain single ones, so the doubled form is matched first and a bold marker is never counted as two italic markers. Underscores and backticks are distinct characters, and the capitals form uses no marker characters at all, so it cannot sit inside any of the other four.

options: Set the asides with unspaced em dashes.
Set the asides with spaced em dashes.
Set the asides with spaced en dashes.
Set the asides with double hyphens instead.
Set the asides with paired commas instead.
task: Edit the discussion section before it goes to the reviewers.
why: The em dash and the en dash are different codepoints, and the surrounding spaces are part of the label, so an unspaced and a spaced em dash are two labels rather than one rendering. The double hyphen is a two-character ASCII stand-in that neither dash matches, and paired commas contain no dash at all.

options: Replace each secret with a fixed asterisk run.
Replace each secret but keep the last four.
Replace each secret with a literal redacted marker.
Replace each secret with a short hash digest.
Leave each secret out of the bundle entirely.
task: Write the connection details into the support bundle.
why: Keeping the last four leaves a mask run in front of it, so it is matched before the full mask, which requires no surviving characters from the original. Omission is the absence of the field, which no replacement value can also satisfy, and the digest is a hex run carrying no mask characters.

options: Write the tags as a bracketed flow list.
Write the tags as a dashed block list.
Write the tags as one comma separated string.
Write the tags as one space separated string.
Write the tags as one repeated tag key.
task: Set the front matter on the new blog post.
why: The label reads the shape of the value bound to the tags key: a bracketed sequence, a dashed block, a single scalar, or a key appearing more than once. The two scalar forms are split by the character between the tags, and a bracketed list is never read as a comma string because the brackets are matched first.

options: Put the code and message at the top level.
Nest the code and message under an error key.
Return a single errors array, even for one failure.
Return a problem object with type, title and detail.
Return an object keyed by the offending field names.
task: Write the body we send back when a request fails validation.
why: An errors array whose single member carries a code and a message contains the flat shape inside it, so the top-level container is read first and only a payload whose code sits at the root is labelled flat. The field-keyed map and the nested error key are both objects one level deep, split on whether the single wrapper key is literally 'error'; a body with both an error wrapper and a root-level code returns 'other'.

options: Answer 204 with no body, exactly as before.
Answer 404, since that order no longer exists.
Answer 200 with a short confirmation body again.
Answer 410, marking the order permanently gone.
Answer 202, queueing the removal work once more.
task: Answer a delete for an order that was already deleted last week.
why: The label reads the status line and nothing else, so the body that accompanies three of these five never changes it; that matters because the 200 and 202 answers both carry text a classifier could otherwise read as a second signal. Each code is a distinct integer, and no response carries two.

options: Print every header name in lowercase with hyphens.
Print every header name title cased with hyphens.
Print every header name in capitals with hyphens.
Print every header name in capitals with underscores.
Print every header name camel cased, no separators.
task: Write out the header names for the integration reference page.
why: The separator is read before the casing — hyphen, underscore or nothing — so a lowercase underscored name is never scored against the lowercase hyphenated label even though the letters match. Among the hyphenated forms the comparison runs case-sensitively across the whole name, and a page mixing two forms returns 'other'.

options: Repeat the key once for each value.
Join the values with commas, one key.
Repeat the key with empty brackets appended.
Repeat the key with numbered brackets appended.
Join the values with pipes, one key.
task: Encode the chosen tag filters into the search request's query string.
why: The numbered form contains the same bracket pair the empty form uses, so what sits between the brackets is read before the brackets are accepted: nothing means the repeated bracket form, a digit means the indexed one. The two joined forms send the key once and are split on the character between values, which neither repeated form ever emits.

options: Send the parameter with the word true.
Send the parameter with the digit one.
Send the parameter name alone, no equals.
Send the parameter with an empty value.
Send the parameter with the word enabled.
task: Pass the include-archived switch through to the listing endpoint.
why: Bare presence and the empty value differ by exactly one character, the equals sign, so the label is read off the raw query string before any parser normalises a valueless key into an empty string — that normalisation is what would collapse the two into one label. The three valued forms are compared literally, so the word true is never folded onto the digit.

options: Put the version in the leading path segment.
Put the version in a required query parameter.
Put the version in a dedicated request header.
Put the version in the accepted media type.
Put the version in the service host name.
task: Decide where the major version sits for the new orders service.
why: The media-type form also puts its version inside a header value, so the dedicated-header label is reserved for a header whose only job is the version, and a version riding as a parameter on Accept is read as the media-type form instead. The path and host labels both live in the request target and are split on whether the version appears in the authority or after the first slash.

options: Send it in Authorization using the Bearer scheme.
Send it in Authorization using the Token scheme.
Send it in Authorization using the Basic scheme.
Send it in a dedicated api key header.
Send it in a signed first-party session cookie.
task: Say how a caller presents its credential to the partner gateway.
why: Three forms share one header and differ only in the scheme word, which is compared as a whole token, so a credential sent with no scheme word at all is none of the three rather than the first of them. The key header and the cookie carry no scheme, and a request presenting two carriers returns 'other' instead of the more specific one.

options: Read the requested type from the Accept header.
Read the requested type from a format parameter.
Read the requested type from the path extension.
Read the requested type from a custom header.
Publish two separate endpoints instead, one type each.
task: Decide how callers pick between JSON and CSV when they export.
why: A request may legally carry an Accept header and a format parameter at once, so the label reads which carrier the server actually honoured rather than which ones arrived; the fixture request deliberately sends both. The separate-endpoint label negotiates nothing, so it is assigned only when no header, parameter or extension is consulted at all.

options: State freshness as a max-age directive alone.
State freshness as an s-maxage directive alone.
State freshness as an absolute Expires date.
State freshness as max-age plus a stale-while-revalidate window.
State freshness as immutable with a long max-age.
task: Set how long the product catalogue response may be reused.
why: Three of the five write a max-age token, so the label reads the whole directive list rather than the presence of that token: the plain form must carry it and nothing beside it, the immutable form must carry the immutable token too, and the revalidation form must carry the stale window. Expires is a different header, and a response sending both headers returns 'other'.

options: Set SameSite to Lax and nothing further.
Set SameSite to Strict and nothing further.
Set SameSite to None alongside the Secure attribute.
Set SameSite to Lax under a host prefix.
Set SameSite to Lax with the Partitioned attribute.
task: Set the session cookie the gateway returns to the dashboard and the embedded widget.
why: Three of the five set the value to Lax, so the plain Lax label is granted only when no decoration accompanies it: the cookie name's host prefix and the Partitioned attribute are each checked before the SameSite value is read. Strict and None are different tokens in that one attribute, and no cookie can be issued carrying two.

options: Carry it in a dedicated request header.
Carry it as a top-level body field.
Carry it as a query string parameter.
Carry it as the final path segment.
Derive it from a hash of the body.
task: Say where a client puts the key that makes a payment retry safe.
why: The four explicit carriers are places in one request, so a request putting the key in two of them returns 'other' rather than the first one found — worth stating because a client-chosen path segment is routinely echoed as an id in the body as well. The derived label requires no explicit key anywhere, so it can never sit underneath one of the others.

options: Send the media type with no charset.
Append charset equals utf-8, lowercase, no space.
Append charset equals UTF-8, uppercase, no space.
Append charset equals utf-8 after one space.
Append charset equals utf-8, the value quoted.
task: Write the Content-Type the JSON endpoints send on every response.
why: The four present forms are compared as raw bytes after the semicolon rather than as parsed parameters, because a conforming parser folds the case, drops the optional space and strips the quotes — which would collapse all four onto one label. The absent form carries no semicolon at all, so it cannot be read as any of them.

options: Return the plain generic JSON media type.
Return a vendor tree type suffixed with json.
Return a resource named subtype suffixed with json.
Return generic JSON carrying a version parameter.
Return generic JSON carrying a schema parameter.
task: Name the media type the orders endpoint returns for version three.
why: The two parameterised forms have an identical type and subtype and are split on the parameter name, so the label reads the whole header value instead of stopping at the slash. The two suffixed forms both end in the json suffix and are split on whether the subtype opens with the vendor tree marker; the generic form has neither a suffix nor a parameter.

options: Declare every collection route with a trailing slash.
Declare every collection route without a trailing slash.
Declare the bare form as an alias.
Declare the slash form as an alias.
Declare one pattern with an optional slash.
task: Write the route table entries for the collection endpoints.
why: Every option is a property of the declared route paths themselves, readable off the table the response emits. One optional-slash pattern is tested first, because a single entry ending in an optional-slash group would otherwise read as a bare path. The two alias forms are tested next, since a table carrying both spellings is not a table carrying only one; which of the pair is marked as the alias separates them. Only then are the single-form labels decided, by whether every declared path ends in a slash or none does. A table mixing bare and slashed paths with no alias marker satisfies none of the five.

options: Send three headers under an X prefix.
Send the same three headers with no prefix.
Send one header carrying all three values.
Send the numbers inside a body meta object.
Send nothing until the limit is actually breached.
task: Tell callers how much of their hourly quota is left.
why: The unprefixed names are exact substrings of the prefixed ones, so the leading vendor prefix is tested before the name is matched and a prefixed response is never counted as unprefixed as well. The single structured header carries the same three quantities inside one value and the meta object carries them in the body, so a response holding two carriers returns 'other'.

options: Give Retry-After as a whole number of seconds.
Give Retry-After as an absolute HTTP date.
Give a delay in milliseconds in the body.
Give an absolute retry timestamp in the body.
Give the delay in a custom milliseconds header.
task: Tell a throttled worker when it may try the call again.
why: The standard header legally holds either an integer or a date, so the two header labels are split on whether its value parses as digits alone; the two body labels are split the same way, a relative count against an absolute instant. The custom header is keyed to its own name, so a response sending it beside the standard one returns 'other' rather than the standard label.

options: Cut every event timestamp at whole seconds.
Cut every event timestamp at three decimals.
Cut every event timestamp at six decimals.
Cut every event timestamp at nine decimals.
Cut every event timestamp at whole minutes.
task: Fix how precise the event times are in the stream we publish.
why: Each shorter rendering is a leading prefix of every longer one, so the label counts the digits after the decimal point exactly rather than testing that a fractional part is present; three written zeroes are the millisecond label and not the whole-second one. The minute form is the only rendering with no seconds field at all.

options: Return 200 with a partial boolean flag set.
Return 200 with the failures listed in errors.
Return 206 to mark the whole response incomplete.
Return 207 with a per-source status for each.
Return 200 with a Warning header naming it.
task: Answer a fan-out read where one of the three backends timed out.
why: The status line is read first and the body only when that status is 200, so a 206 carrying a partial flag as well is labelled by its status and never counted twice. Among the three 200 forms the carriers differ — a boolean field, an errors array, a response header — and a response using two of them returns 'other'.

options: Send nothing back in the response body.
Send back the whole record that was deleted.
Send back the deleted record's id only.
Send back a count of rows removed.
Send back a short human readable status message.
task: Decide what comes back when a delete actually removes something.
why: The id appears inside the echoed record too, so the label counts how many of the record's fields are present rather than looking for the id: the echo carries the whole row, the id label exactly one field. The count holds a number under a differently named key, and the empty label requires zero bytes of body.

options: Return one result per input, in order.
Return an object keyed by each input id.
Return succeeded and failed in separate arrays.
Return only the failures, silence meaning success.
Return one verdict, rejecting the batch on failure.
task: Report what happened to each row in a two-hundred-row import.
why: When every row succeeds the failures-only form is an empty array and the split form has an empty failed array, so the label reads which keys are present rather than what they hold: the split label requires a succeeded key and the failures-only label forbids one. The keyed object and the ordered array are separated by whether positions or ids address the results.

options: Report a percentage complete as one number.
Report processed and total as two counts.
Report the name of the current stage.
Report only the coarse state, nothing finer.
Report an estimated finish time, nothing else.
task: Say how the long-running reindex reports its progress to pollers.
why: Counts and a percentage express the same fraction, so the label reads which fields the response actually holds rather than what a client could derive from them, and a response carrying both returns 'other'. The coarse-state label requires none of the finer fields to be present, so it can never sit beneath one of the other four.

options: Put it in one dedicated signature header.
Put it in a signature and timestamp pair.
Put it in Authorization under a signing scheme.
Put it in a field of the envelope.
Put it in a query parameter on delivery.
task: Say where the delivery signature rides on an outbound webhook.
why: The paired form also emits a signature header, so the companion timestamp header is looked for before the single-header label is granted; without that order every paired delivery would match both labels. The envelope field sits inside the signed body and the parameter sits in the request target, so neither can be read as a header.

options: Put the reserved keys beside the payload fields.
Put the payload under data, metadata above it.
Put the metadata and payload in sibling objects.
Put the metadata in transport headers, payload alone.
Put the payload under a type-named key.
task: Fix the envelope every service publishes its domain events inside.
why: Three forms nest the payload one level down and are split on the wrapper key alone: the literal word data, a pair of sibling objects, or a key named for the event type. The flat form has no wrapper, and the sidecar form's message body is the bare payload, so the metadata it relies on never appears in the JSON the label reads.

options: Name each type as dotted lowercase words.
Name each type with a colon separator.
Name each type with a slash separator.
Name each type as past tense PascalCase.
Name each type in screaming snake capitals.
task: Name the event types the new publisher will emit.
why: Four of the five join the two words with a character — a dot, a colon, a slash or an underscore — and those are compared literally, so no name matches two labels. The fifth joins nothing at all and is told apart from the underscored form by case as well as by separator, so a capitalised dotted name returns 'other'.

options: Republish the bytes unchanged, reason in the headers.
Wrap the original message inside a failure envelope.
Add a failure field to the original body.
Write a separate reason record beside the message.
Change nothing, letting the topic name carry it.
task: Mark the messages the consumer gives up on after five attempts.
why: The envelope contains the original body inside it, so the outer shape is read before any field is looked for: an envelope carrying its own reason field is the wrapper label and never the injected-field one. The header and topic labels both leave the body byte-identical and are split on whether any header was added.

options: Emit every field, using null when unset.
Omit any field that has no value.
Emit null for scalars, empty for collections.
Omit them, listing the omitted names separately.
Emit the type's zero value instead of null.
task: Settle how an unset optional field looks in the profile response.
why: Two forms write nulls and are split on what happens to unset arrays and objects, so the fixture record carries at least one unset field of each kind: the mixed form must show an empty collection exactly where the plain form shows null. Two forms drop the field and are split on whether a list of omitted names accompanies them, and the zero-value form writes no nulls anywhere.

options: Send a deprecation header on affected responses.
Rename the field with a deprecated suffix.
Add a warning object to the response body.
Ship the replacement field beside it, both populated.
Add a removal date field to the record.
task: Emit the account payload while the old address field retires.
why: All five markers now live in the one payload the response emits, so the label reads which carrier holds the notice. The header sits outside the body and is tested first. A warning object is tested before the two field-level forms, because a payload may carry both and the object is the declared notice. The parallel replacement is two populated fields under related names; the suffix form is one field whose name ends in the marker. The removal date is a dated field on the record and is tested last, since any of the other four may also carry a date.

options: Ship an explicit unknown member for future values.
Type the field as a plain open string.
Use numeric codes with gaps reserved for growth.
Number the members densely from one upward.
Declare a reserved block beside the current members.
task: Decide how the shipment status list grows over the next few releases.
why: All five are properties of the single declaration the response emits. A reserved block is a declaration of its own and is tested first, because a list may carry one alongside any numbering. A catch-all member is tested next, since it is a named member the other forms do not emit. The open string declares no members at all. The two numeric forms are separated last and only by arithmetic on the emitted values: consecutive from one is dense, anything leaving a gap is not. A list of named members with neither a catch-all nor a reserved block satisfies none of the five.

options: Put an exact total in the body metadata.
Put an exact total in a response header.
Put an estimated total in the body metadata.
Put a boolean saying whether more pages remain.
Put a link pointing at the last page.
task: Say what the search endpoint reveals beyond the page it returns.
why: The exact and the estimated total are both integers sitting in the same place, split on the field name, which the fixture spells differently — a checker keyed on the value's type alone would merge them. The header form moves that number out of the body entirely, and the boolean and the link carry no count anywhere.

options: Prefix the field name with a minus.
Follow the field name with a colon.
Send the direction in its own parameter.
Put the field in brackets, direction as value.
Send field and direction as one spaced string.
task: Pin down how a client asks for newest first on the listing endpoint.
why: The bracketed form and the separate-parameter form both send the bare direction word as a value, so they are split on whether the parameter name carries the field inside brackets rather than on the value itself. The spaced string is the only value holding whitespace, and the sign and colon forms are single tokens told apart by the character they carry.

options: Put the operator in brackets after the field.
Join the operator to the field with underscores.
Send one filter parameter holding an expression string.
Send one filter parameter holding an encoded object.
Give each operator its own named query parameter.
task: Let callers ask for orders above a value on the listing endpoint.
why: The two single-parameter forms share one parameter name and are split on the first character of its decoded value: a brace opens the object form, anything else is the expression. The two decorated-field forms differ in whether the operator sits inside brackets or behind underscores, and the dedicated parameter carries no operator token at all.

options: Take a comma separated list of field names.
Take a brace nested expression over the tree.
Take an array of pointers in the body.
Take a Prefer header asking for minimal representations.
Take a named view like summary or full.
task: Let a client ask for a trimmed version of the record.
why: The brace expression holds a comma separated run of names inside its braces, so the opening brace is looked for before any comma is read; without that order every nested mask would satisfy the flat list as well. The pointer array and the two header-borne forms sit in different parts of the request, and a request carrying two of them returns 'other'.

options: Give a dotted path from the root.
Give a slash separated pointer from the root.
Give a path with bracketed array indexes.
Give the leaf field name on its own.
Give the name plus where it lives.
task: Point at the exact field that failed inside a nested order payload.
why: The dotted and the bracketed path join objects the same way and are separated only by how an array index is written, so the fixture's failing field is required to sit inside an array — without one the two forms produce an identical string. The pointer opens with a slash neither path form allows, and the leaf name carries no separator at all.

options: Redirect permanently with 301, letting methods change.
Redirect permanently with 308, preserving the original method.
Redirect temporarily with 302, letting methods change.
Redirect temporarily with 307, preserving the original method.
Redirect with 303, sending every caller to GET.
task: Handle requests still arriving at the old reports path.
why: The label reads the status code alone, so the method rules named beside each one are explanation rather than part of the match; that is what keeps the two permanent codes apart even though a client following either lands on the same path. No response carries two status codes.

options: Require an If-Match header carrying the entity tag.
Require an If-Unmodified-Since header carrying the last time.
Require a version number field in the body.
Require an expected state object in the body.
Require a version number in a custom header.
task: Stop two editors overwriting each other on the same document.
why: Two guards ride in the body and are split on shape, a scalar beside the payload against a nested object of expected values, while two ride in standard headers with different names. The custom header carries the same kind of version the body scalar does, so the label reads where the guard sits rather than what it holds, and a request sending two returns 'other'.

options: Carry the version in an envelope field.
Carry the version in a message header.
Carry the version in prefixed magic bytes.
Carry the version in the topic name.
Carry the version in the content type.
task: Say how a consumer learns which schema a message was written against.
why: The envelope field and the prefixed bytes both sit inside the message value and are split on whether the version can be read before the payload is parsed at all. The header, the topic and the content type all sit outside the value, and a producer stamping the version in two places returns 'other' rather than the innermost one.

options: Encode it as standard padded base64 text.
Encode it in the url-safe alphabet, unpadded.
Encode it as a data scheme string.
Encode it as an array of integers.
Encode it as a compact base85 string.
task: Carry the short device attestation blob inside the JSON claim.
why: The url-safe alphabet is a subset of the standard one, so a blob whose bytes never produce a plus or a slash would satisfy both labels; the fixture blob is chosen to produce both characters, and the padding is compared as well. The data-scheme string contains a base64 run inside it, so its scheme and media type are matched before the encoding is read.

options: Negotiate with Accept-Encoding and vary the response.
Compress always, declaring it without any negotiation.
Compress the body and mark a custom header.
Compress one field and base64 it inside.
Name the codec in the media type.
task: Decide how the bulk export deals with compressing what it sends.
why: The negotiated and the always-on forms both emit a content encoding header, so the label turns on whether the response also varies on the request's accepted encodings, which the always-on form never does. The field-level form leaves the message itself uncompressed, and the transport form emits no encoding header anywhere.

options: Echo the caller's id in the same header.
Echo the caller's id in a correlation header.
Echo the caller's id in the error body.
Echo it in both a header and body.
Ignore theirs and return a freshly minted id.
task: Give the desk a way to trace one call through the gateway.
why: The both-carriers label is tested before either single one, since a response holding the value in a header and in the body would otherwise match two. The two header labels are split on the name used, the caller's own against a differently named one, and the minted label requires the returned value to differ from whatever arrived.

options: Send the next cursor back as null.
Leave the next cursor key out entirely.
Send a boolean saying no more remain.
Send an empty string as the cursor.
Send a remaining count reading exactly zero.
task: Handle the last page of the activity feed.
why: The null cursor, the empty string and the missing key are three distinct states of one field that any falsy check would merge into one, so the label reads the raw payload before a client's coercion touches it. The boolean and the count are separate fields, split on type, and a page carrying two of the five markers returns 'other'.

options: POST to a cancel sub-path under the order.
PATCH the order, setting its status to cancelled.
POST to a shared actions collection naming both.
PUT a cancellation sub-resource under the order.
POST to the order carrying a command field.
task: Expose cancelling an order that has not shipped yet.
why: Two forms write to a child path under the order and are split on the method, two target the order itself and are split the same way, and the shared collection sits at the root instead. The label therefore reads method and target together, and one request carries exactly one of each, so no pair of labels can both apply.

options: Send only the fields that are changing.
Send an ordered array of edit operations.
Send the whole record with the change applied.
Send changed fields plus an explicit field mask.
Send both the previous and the new values.
task: Fix what an update to one field of a customer record looks like.
why: The merge body and the masked body both hold changed fields at the top level, so the presence of the mask key is checked first; without that order every masked update would satisfy the merge label too. The operation list is an array rather than an object, and the replacement and the pair forms are split on whether an untouched field appears once or twice.

options: Nest an object keyed by relation name.
Nest an array of relation and target pairs.
Send the relations as Link response headers.
Put flat target fields at the top level.
Send identifiers only and let clients build.
task: Decide how the invoice list points callers at related records.
why: The keyed object and the array of pairs both hang off the same links key and are split on whether that value opens as an object or as a list, which is the one place a checker reading only the key name would score twice. The flat fields sit beside the record's own data, the header form puts nothing in the body, and the identifier form carries no target at all.

options: Return a lowercase ok and nothing else.
Return the word healthy in plain lowercase.
Return UP in capitals, as monitors expect.
Return the word pass, borrowed from checks.
Return the colour word green in lowercase.
task: Choose the word the readiness endpoint returns when everything is fine.
why: The five words are compared whole and case-sensitively, so the capitalised form is a different label from the same letters in lower case and one probe can never match two. A body carrying a status word plus a second synonym returns 'other' rather than whichever appears first.

options: Use uppercase underscored symbols for every code.
Use dotted lowercase namespaces for every code.
Use bare integers drawn from one range.
Use a short letter prefix plus digits.
Use the HTTP status number as the code.
task: Give each billing failure a stable code the client can branch on.
why: Two forms are digits alone and are split on range: the status reuse must be a valid three-digit status, and the application integers are drawn from a band the fixture puts well outside that space. The prefixed form carries digits behind letters, so the leading letters are read first, and the two word forms differ in separator and case.

options: Write one JSON object per newline delimited line.
Write each row as a server-sent event block.
Write a byte length before every row.
Write one JSON array streamed in chunks.
Write each row inside a multipart boundary.
task: Frame the rows the export stream sends over one long connection.
why: The line-delimited and the chunked-array forms both send JSON objects the reader separates by scanning bytes, and they are split on whether the stream opens with an array bracket. The event blocks prefix every line with a field name, and the length prefix and the boundary marker are non-JSON framing read before any row is parsed.

options: Take a from and a to parameter.
Take a since and an until parameter.
Take a start plus a duration length.
Take one parameter holding an interval string.
Take one relative keyword naming the window.
task: Let an analyst pull the readings recorded inside a chosen window.
why: The two bounded pairs carry the same two instants and are separated only by the parameter names, matched literally, so a request mixing one name from each pair returns 'other' rather than the closer match. The two single-parameter forms are split on whether the value holds two timestamps joined by a slash or a keyword with no digits.

options: Nest the item path under its order.
Keep items at the root, parent as filter.
Keep items at the root, addressed alone.
Join both ids into one composite segment.
Expose items only inside the order's whole representation.
task: Settle the path shape for a line item on the orders service.
why: The two root-level forms share an identical path and are split on whether a parent parameter rides in the query, so a flat path carrying the order id is never read as the global form. The composite segment holds both ids inside one segment where the nested form spends two, and the aggregate label is granted only when no path addresses an item at all.

options: Leave deleted rows out of every response.
Include them carrying a deleted boolean flag.
Include them carrying a deletion timestamp field.
Include a tombstone holding the id only.
Exclude them and answer 410 on fetches.
task: Decide how soft-deleted rows are handled when the accounts endpoint is read.
why: The two hiding labels both keep the row out of the listing and are separated by what a direct fetch of that id returns, so the fixture exercises both calls rather than the listing alone. The flag and the timestamp are different fields on an otherwise whole record, and the tombstone is told apart by carrying no other fields.

options: Send an Age header on cached responses.
Send a custom hit or miss header.
Send the answer in a body meta field.
Send a Server-Timing entry naming the lookup.
Send the serving node's identifier in a header.
task: Settle what the edge tier says about where a response came from.
why: An age header and a timing entry can both appear on one response for unrelated reasons, so each label requires its own carrier to be the thing stating the outcome, and a response stating it twice returns 'other'. Two options are custom headers and are separated by content, not by carrier: the hit-or-miss form carries one of those two words and is tested first, and the node form carries an identifier and no verdict. Every label requires a carrier to be present, so a response disclosing nothing satisfies none of them.

options: Pin the exact version with no operator.
Allow later minors behind a caret operator.
Allow later patches behind a tilde operator.
Write an explicit lower and upper bound.
Write the patch position as a wildcard.
task: Write the version constraint for the library we are adding this week.
why: The operator token is read before any digits are looked at, which matters because a caret on a zero-major version resolves to the same set of releases a tilde would: the label records what was written, never what the resolver worked out. The comparator form is the only one carrying two operators, and a constraint mixing a caret with a comparator returns 'other'.

options: Wrap each name in doubled curly braces.
Wrap each name in dollar and braces.
Wrap each name in paired percent signs.
Wrap each name in paired angle brackets.
Prefix each name with a bare dollar.
task: Mark the substitution points in the new service scaffold files.
why: The dollar-and-braces form contains a brace pair, so the plain doubled-brace label is granted only when no sigil precedes the opening brace; the bare dollar form is the mirror case, requiring a dollar with no brace after it. The percent and angle forms use characters none of the other three touch.

options: Open each name with the word should.
Write each name as given, when, then.
Open each name with the word test.
Write each name as a descriptive sentence.
Open each name with the method exercised.
task: Name the tests you are adding for the discount calculator.
why: The clause form is a descriptive sentence too, so the plain-sentence label is assigned only when none of the three clause markers appears anywhere in the name. The two opening-word labels are read from the first token alone, and a name opening with one word and carrying clause markers later returns 'other'.

options: Put a note on the line above each setting.
Put a note at the end of each line.
Put one explaining block at the top of the file.
Put a banner note above each group of settings.
Put one explaining block after all of the settings.
task: Add the explanatory notes to the worker configuration file.
why: The trailing form and the above-line form use the same comment marker, so the label reads whether a setting shares the line with its note rather than looking for the marker itself. A file carrying a header block and per-setting notes returns 'other', which is the realistic mixed case here. The header and footer forms use the same block shape and are separated only by whether any setting precedes it, so every option requires a comment to be present somewhere in the file.

options: Separate the words with hyphens after two dashes.
Separate the words with underscores after two dashes.
Join the words in camel case after dashes.
Run the words together, unseparated, after two dashes.
Write the whole option after a single dash.
task: Spell the multi-word options for the command line tool you are writing.
why: The dash count is read before the separator, so the single-dash form is never scored against any of the four two-dash labels even when the letters after the dashes match one of them exactly. The run-together and camel forms differ only in capitalisation and are compared case-sensitively.

options: Lead the name with the next sequential integer.
Lead the name with a full UTC timestamp.
Lead the name with the date and counter.
Lead the name with the release version number.
Close the name with a short content hash.
task: Name the file for the schema change you are adding this afternoon.
why: The full timestamp and the date-plus-counter form both open with the same eight date digits, so the label reads what follows those digits: an uninterrupted time-of-day run against a separator and a short ordinal. The content hash is the only marker that trails the descriptive words rather than leading them.

options: Join the values with colons in one variable.
Join the values with commas in one variable.
Join the values with spaces in one variable.
Set one numbered variable per value instead.
Store the values as a JSON array.
task: Hand the worker its list of allowed regions through the environment.
why: The JSON string carries commas inside it, so the bracketed form is tested before the comma-joined one and a JSON value is never read as plain comma separation. The numbered form is the only one that sets more than a single variable, which is checked by counting names before any value is parsed.

options: Show a unified diff with three context lines.
Show a unified diff of the whole file.
Show the old and new text side by side.
Show the changed words marked inside each line.
Show only the changed line counts per file.
task: Show the reviewer what changed in the pricing module this week.
why: Word-level marking sits inside an otherwise ordinary hunk, so the label looks for intra-line markers before it counts context lines; without that ordering a word-marked diff would also satisfy the three-line label. The two unified forms are split on whether unchanged lines outside the hunks appear, and the stat form carries no file content at all.

options: Name an environment variable the process reads.
Write a store reference carrying its scheme.
Point at a file the runtime reads.
Write a placeholder the deploy step substitutes.
Store the encrypted value in place.
task: Point the deployment config at the database password.
why: The store reference and the file pointer both render as locators, so the label tests for a scheme prefix before the slashes: a bare path is the file form and only a path carrying its own scheme is the store form. The substituted placeholder never survives into the deployed file, so it is read from the checked-in text rather than the running config.

options: Open every name with the word mock.
Open every name with the word fake.
Open every name with the word stub.
Close every name with the word double.
Open every name with the words in memory.
task: Name the replacement objects the checkout suite uses for the gateway.
why: The three leading words are distinct tokens matched against the first word only, so a class whose body behaves like one kind but is named another is labelled by its name. The trailing word is read from the last token, and a name opening with one of the three and closing with the suffix returns 'other'.

options: Write the bare directory name on its own.
Anchor the pattern with a leading slash.
Close the pattern with a trailing slash.
Write a globstar path down to contents.
Ignore everything, then unignore what you keep.
task: Tell the tooling to leave the build output tree alone.
why: The leading slash and the trailing slash are independent decorations that a single pattern can legally carry at once, so each label requires exactly one of them and a pattern carrying both returns 'other'. The bare name carries neither, and the globstar form is recognised by the doubled star rather than by any slash.

options: Write one plain sentence and nothing else.
Open the entry with a category word.
Open the entry with the component name.
Close the entry with the ticket key.
Close the entry with the contributor handle.
task: Add an entry for the caching fix to the release notes file.
why: Both leading forms occupy the same position, so the opening token is matched against the closed list of change kinds first and read as a component name only when it fails that list. An entry carrying a leading token and a trailing one returns 'other' rather than the more specific of the two.

options: Flatten each nested key using single underscores.
Flatten each nested key using doubled underscores.
Flatten each nested key into dotted lowercase.
Flatten each nested key into joined camel.
Pass the whole block as one variable.
task: Expose the nested settings block to the container as environment variables.
why: A single underscore is a substring of a doubled one, so the separator run is counted exactly rather than merely detected; without that the doubled form would also satisfy the single one on every name. The dotted form is the only lowercase rendering, and the packed form sets one name whose value opens with a brace.

options: Return zero on success and one otherwise.
Split findings from tool errors across two codes.
Give each finding category its own code.
Return the number of findings that were seen.
Draw the failure codes from a reserved range.
task: Decide what the repository check wrapper returns to the shell.
why: A run with exactly one finding returns 1 under both the binary scheme and the counting scheme, so the label is read from the documented mapping rather than from any single observed exit, and the reference run deliberately has three findings. The reserved-range scheme never emits 1 at all.

options: Chain the expectation onto the value tested.
Call an equality helper with expected and actual.
Assert on a bare boolean comparison expression.
Pass a matcher object into one assert call.
Attach a should property to the value itself.
task: Write the checks inside the new invoice rounding tests.
why: The chained form and the property form both read left to right from the value under test, so the label looks at whether the first member after the value is a call or a bare attribute, which is the only thing separating them. The matcher form always passes its comparison in as an argument, so it can never be mistaken for either chain.

options: List each path, then the team beside it.
List each team, then its paths beneath it.
Open with a catch-all line, then exceptions.
Group the paths under commented section headings.
Name one owning team for the whole repository.
task: Write down who reviews which parts of this repository.
why: All five are shapes of the one file the response emits. The first two contain exactly the same tokens and are ordered opposites, so the label reads which token opens each record instead of which tokens are present. The catch-all form is tested before them, because its later records are path-then-team lines and would otherwise be read as that form; what marks it is a first record matching everything. The commented-heading form is tested next, since its records may take either order and only the headings distinguish it. The single-owner form is one record naming no path.

options: Name each fixture by its bare noun.
Lead each fixture name with its validity.
Lead each fixture name with an article.
Close each fixture name with its purpose.
Number the fixture names within each noun.
task: Name the sample payment records the settlement tests load.
why: A validity word and an article both sit in front of the noun, so the leading token is matched against a short closed article list first and treated as a validity word only when it is not an article. A name carrying a leading decoration and a trailing number returns 'other' rather than either label.

options: Add a key and colon trailer line.
Put a bracketed token on the subject line.
Put the bare key inside the subject text.
End the body with a closing prose sentence.
Add a key and equals sign footer line.
task: Record which ticket the commit you are about to make closes.
