why: The two final-line forms differ by a single separator character in the same position and are compared literally, since a parser that accepts both would collapse them onto one label. The two subject forms are split on whether brackets surround the key, and a message carrying a subject token and a final-line trailer returns 'other'.

options: Group by origin: standard library, third party, local.
Sort every import into a single alphabetical block.
Sort the imports by length, shortest line first.
Group the imports by how deep they run.
Keep the type-only imports in a final group.
task: Arrange the import statements at the top of the module you refactored.
why: Several of these are compatible in principle, since origin groups can each be alphabetical inside themselves, so the label reads the top-level partition first and only falls through to within-block ordering when there is a single unbroken block. The length ordering is checked on characters, not on the paths themselves.

options: Use a single identifier line naming the licence.
Paste the full licence text as a comment.
Write a short notice with year and holder.
Point at the licence file kept at root.
Draw a boxed banner around the notice text.
task: Write the licence notice that heads each front-end source file.
why: All five are forms of the one header the response emits, so the label is read off that header's own text. The full text runs to many lines and is tested first, because a boxed banner or a short notice can appear inside it. The banner is tested next, on its rule characters, since the line it frames may itself be a short notice. The reference form names a file and states no year; the short form states a year and a holder and names no file; the identifier form is a single tagged token carrying neither. A header carrying two of these returns 'other'.

options: Name each target with a bare verb.
Write the verb, a colon, then noun.
Write the noun, a colon, then verb.
Join the parts with dots into namespaces.
Join the parts with slashes into paths.
task: Name the entries in the repository task runner file.
why: The two colon forms use identical punctuation and are separated only by which side of it the verb sits on, so the label reads the roles of the two tokens rather than the character between them. The bare verb has no separator, and the dotted and slashed forms differ in one character that neither colon form emits.

options: Write the bare marker word and the note.
Attach the owner in round brackets afterwards.
Attach the ticket key in square brackets afterwards.
Attach a review-by date after the marker word.
Put the marker alone above the explaining line.
task: Leave a reminder in the code about the retry path you shortcut.
why: The owner and the ticket decorations differ in bracket character rather than in content, and are compared on that character alone, because a short ticket key can read as a name and a name can read as a key. A marker carrying two decorations returns 'other' rather than whichever comes first. The bare form and the next-line form both carry no decoration and are separated by whether the note shares the marker's line, so all five require the marker word to be present.

options: One root file with glob-headed sections.
One root file keyed by language.
One file grouped by rule severity.
One flat rule set for everything.
One ordered list where later entries win.
task: Decide how the shared editor settings apply across this repository.
why: All five are shapes of the one settings file the response emits. Three cut the file into sections and are separated by what the section head is: a path pattern, a language name, or a severity word. The remaining two carry no heads at all, and are told apart by whether any setting name appears more than once -- the ordered form repeats a key so a later entry can win, the flat form states each key exactly once. That is what stops the flat form being read as a degenerate case of any other.

options: Give every package one shared scope prefix.
Name packages with dotted domain style segments.
Echo the directory path with dashes between.
Give each package a bare short name.
Open each package name with its layer.
task: Name the packages as you split the application into a workspace.
why: The shared scope and the layer marker both open the name with a common token, so the label checks whether that token is constant across every package or varies with the package's tier. The path-echoing form is derived from the tree, so a name that both matches its directory path and carries a leading token returns 'other'.

options: Name the upstream project on its own line.
Give the upstream version and the copy date.
List any local patches applied since copying.
Warn in capitals that the file is generated.
Record a checksum of the copied file.
task: Stamp the third-party source file we copied in last week.
why: All five are lines the emitted stamp either carries or does not, so one stamp gets one label. The capitalised warning is tested first, because a stamp that carries it is declaring itself generated whatever else it names. The checksum is a hexadecimal run no other line produces. The version-and-date line carries two values where the name line carries one, so the name line is tested after it -- a stamp naming the project and its version is the version form, not the name form. The patch list is the only line that may be empty and still present, so it is matched on its heading rather than its contents.

options: A usage line, then the flag list.
The flag list, then worked examples.
A two column table of flag meanings.
A few paragraphs of plain prose.
Numbered sections in the manual page order.
task: Lay out what the tool prints when someone asks for help.
why: A usage line and a worked example are both single lines of sample invocation, so the label reads their position relative to the flag list rather than trying to tell the two apart by content. The table and prose forms are split on whether flag names occupy a column of their own.

options: Open each file with a do-not-edit banner.
Put a generated marker inside each file name.
Give the files an extra extension segment.
List the files in a sibling manifest.
Keep the files in their own directory.
task: Mark the client code the schema tool writes on every build.
why: The infix marker and the extra extension both change the file name, so the label reads where the added token sits relative to the final dot rather than merely detecting it. The banner leaves the name untouched, and a file carrying a banner and a marked name returns 'other'.

options: Name each job by its verb alone.
Open each job name with its stage.
Close each job name with its platform.
Name each job after the tool run.
Number the job names in run order.
task: Name the jobs in the pipeline definition you are adding.
why: A tool name often reads as a verb as well, so the token is matched against the pipeline's declared tool list before the bare-verb label is considered. A name carrying a leading stage word and a trailing platform word returns 'other' rather than either single label.

options: Take everything as ordered positional arguments.
Take everything as named long flags.
Take a subcommand first, then flags.
Take everything from the environment instead.
Take one path to a config.
task: Decide how the release helper script takes what it needs.
why: The subcommand form carries flags too, so the label reads whether the first non-flag word selects behaviour before any flags are counted; otherwise every subcommand invocation would also satisfy the flags label. The config-file form takes exactly one positional path, so argument count separates it from the positional form.

options: List every member path out in full.
Write one single-star glob for the folder.
Write one double-star glob covering everything nested.
Write one glob per architectural layer folder.
Write a broad glob with one exclusion.
task: Declare which directories the root manifest treats as members.
why: The one-star and two-star globs differ by a single character in the same position, so the label counts stars rather than testing that a star is present. The per-layer form is several one-star globs, so it is separated from the single glob by how many entries the list holds, not by their shape. The exclusion form is tested first, because it also contains a glob and would otherwise be read as whichever star count it happens to use. Every option requires at least one member entry to be declared.

options: Use bare verbs with nothing appended.
Scope the names with colons between parts.
Scope the names with dashes between parts.
Open the names with their lifecycle phase.
Write the multi-word names in camel case.
task: Name the commands you are adding to the front-end package manifest.
why: A lifecycle prefix is itself joined with a dash in practice, so a dashed name is checked against the closed lifecycle-word list before the plain dashed label is granted. The colon and dash forms are then compared on the separator character alone, and the camel form carries no separator to compare.

options: Declare both axes and take every combination.
List each wanted combination out in full.
Declare both axes, then exclude the gaps.
Declare one axis, then add extra combinations.
Write separate jobs and skip the matrix.
task: Declare the combinations the test pipeline should run across.
why: The exclusion form and the plain cross product declare identical axes and differ only by a block that may be empty, so the label requires that block to be present and non-empty rather than inferring it from how many jobs actually ran. The explicit list declares no axes at all.

options: One executable script per hook phase.
A declarative list of tools to run.
One dispatcher script reading a registry file.
A shared directory symlinked into place.
One inline command written in the config.
task: Set up the checks that run on this machine before a commit lands.
why: The dispatcher and the declarative list both read their work from a tracked file, so the label reads whether a script the team maintains sits between the hook and the tools. The symlinked directory also holds phase scripts, so it is separated from the per-phase form by whether the files live in the hooks directory or are pointed at from it. The inline form is the only one declaring no file at all, and is tested last, since it is a command written where the other four would name a path.

options: Name each stage after its purpose.
Number the stages in declaration order.
Name each stage after its tool.
Open each stage name with its role.
Leave the stages unnamed, referencing positions.
task: Name the stages in the multi-stage image build file.
why: The purpose name and the role prefix both describe what the stage does, so the label checks whether a token from the closed role list opens the name before reading the rest as a purpose. Numbered stages are digits only, and unnamed stages carry no token for either test to read.

options: Hash the lockfile and use that alone.
Hash the manifest and append the platform.
Include the branch name in the key.
Use a fixed key with prefix fallbacks.
Use the exact commit hash instead.
task: Build the key the pipeline uses to restore its dependency cache.
why: Two of the five are content digests that render identically, so the label reads which file was hashed and whether a platform token trails it, not the hexadecimal itself. The commit digest is a repository digest rather than a file digest, and a key combining a branch name with a file hash returns 'other'.

options: Mark it with the language deprecation attribute.
Mark it with a doc comment tag.
Rename it with a deprecated name suffix.
Emit a runtime warning from inside it.
Leave a comment naming the removal date.
task: Mark the old settings helper so callers move off it.
why: The attribute and the doc tag both sit immediately above the declaration, so the label reads whether the marker is language syntax the compiler sees or comment text it ignores. The rename changes the symbol itself, so a renamed symbol also carrying an attribute returns 'other' rather than the attribute label.

options: Name, version, then the platform triple.
Name plus the short commit hash.
Name, version, then the build number.
Name plus the date it built.
Name alone, with the version inside.
task: Name the archive the release job drops in the output directory.
why: The version and the build number are both digit runs, so the label counts dot-separated fields before reading any of them; a two-field version beside a build number would otherwise read as a three-field version. The short hash is matched on its character class rather than its length, since a build number can be six digits long too.

options: One grouped declaration listing them all together.
A separate declaration beside each such target.
A naming convention the reader recognises instead.
A shared always-stale sentinel dependency on each.
A pattern rule covering the whole group.
task: Declare the targets in the build file that write no file.
why: The grouped and the per-target forms use the identical directive and differ only in how many times it appears and where, so the label counts occurrences against the target count rather than matching the directive once. The sentinel and pattern forms use no directive at all and are separated by whether the extra name is a dependency or a rule head. The naming convention is tested last, since a file using any of the other four may also follow it.

options: Name it after the behaviour it controls.
Open it with the owning team name.
Name it after the ticket that introduced it.
Close it with the date for removal.
Close it with the stage it occupies.
task: Name the flag guarding the new checkout screen in the app.
why: The removal date and the rollout stage are both trailing tokens on a behaviour name, so the label reads what kind of token trails rather than that one does. A name opening with a team token and closing with a stage token returns 'other' instead of the more specific of the two.

options: Open the optional remarks with a nit marker.
Open every remark with a severity word.
Phrase the optional remarks as open questions.
Mark the blocking remarks, leaving others bare.
Keep the optional remarks in the summary.
task: Leave your comments on the branch someone opened this morning.
why: The nit word is itself one member of a severity vocabulary, so the label checks whether every remark carries a word from that list before the severity form is assigned, and treats a single word used only on optional remarks as the narrower label. A review both marking blocking items and prefixing optional ones returns 'other'.

options: Open it with a two digit sequence.
Open it with the package and version.
Name it after the ticket needing it.
Name it after what it changes.
Name it after the upstream commit.
task: Name the patch we keep against the upstream parser in this tree.
why: The sequence prefix and the version prefix both open with digits, so the label tests whether dots separate the digit groups before either is granted. The description and the ticket forms both open with letters and are told apart by matching the leading token against the ticket key shape rather than by meaning.

options: Lowercase, with no full stop anywhere.
Sentence case, closing with a full stop.
Opened by the tool name and colon.
Opened by a stable code, then text.
Closed by a sentence naming the fix.
task: Word the messages the tool prints when something goes wrong.
why: Two of the five put a token before the message text, so the leading token is matched against the program name and then the code list, and the capitalisation and terminal punctuation tests run only once neither matches. Otherwise a prefixed message would also satisfy whichever casing label its first letter happened to fit.

options: In parentheses at the end of each description.
In a separate column beside each option name.
In square brackets inside the description text itself.
Straight after each flag name, before its description.
In one list at the foot of help.
task: Show what each option falls back to when nobody sets it.
why: Round and square brackets both sit inside the description line, so the label compares the bracket characters themselves rather than looking for a bracketed run. The column and footer forms move the value out of the description entirely and are split on whether it sits beside its option or after all of them. The post-name form places the value between the flag and its description with no bracket at all, so it is separated from the column form by whether the columns line up down the block. Every option requires the default to appear somewhere in the help text.

options: Angle-bracketed tokens naming what belongs there.
Empty values with a comment explaining each.
A literal change-me word in every slot.
A commented-out example value above each key.
Null values with a required flag beside.
task: Write the sample config a new joiner copies before filling it in.
why: An empty value and a null value both read as unset once the file is parsed, so the label is taken from the file text rather than the parsed tree, which is the only place they still differ. Two forms carry a comment, and are separated by what sits on the key's own line: the empty form leaves the value blank, the example form fills it in and comments the sample out above. Every key is present in every option, so a file that omitted keys entirely satisfies none of them.

options: A skip annotation carrying the reason inline.
The whole body commented out for now.
A marker prefix added to the name.
An early return behind a condition check.
An expected-failure marker on the test.
task: Park the flaky timezone test until someone can look at it.
why: The skip annotation and the expected-failure marker are both decorators above the test body, so the label reads how the runner reports a body that now passes: skipped in one case, unexpectedly passing in the other. A commented-out body is never collected, so it can carry neither marker. The guarded form carries no decorator at all and is the only one whose skip lives inside the body, so it is tested after both decorators to keep a decorated test that also returns early from reading as a guard.

options: A fixed number of approvals from anyone.
One approval from a listed code owner.
A number of approvals including an owner.
Different rules for different paths in tree.
Green checks only, with no human approval.
task: Write down what a change needs before it lands on the main line.
why: The count-plus-owner rule satisfies the plain count rule on every merge it permits, so the label is read from the written policy rather than from any individual merge that happened to satisfy both. A policy stating a global count and then delegating some paths to their own rules returns 'other'.

options: A small version file at the root.
An engines field in the package manifest.
A pinned image the build runs inside.
A line of prose in the readme.
A setup script that checks and installs.
task: Fix which toolchain version contributors build this project with.
why: The root version file and the manifest field both hold a bare version string, so the label reads which file carries it rather than the string's shape. The setup script states no version of its own, so it is assigned only when the enforced value originates in the script and not in a file the script reads.

options: One long line, however wide it runs.
Backslash continuations, one flag per line.
An arguments array built up, then expanded.
The flags moved into a config file.
The flags held in one expanded variable.
task: Write out the long build invocation inside the repository helper script.
why: The array and the variable both hold the flags in a name expanded at the call site, so the label reads whether the value is a list or a single string, which is exactly the distinction that decides whether a flag containing a space survives. The continuation form still writes every flag at the call site, so no expansion appears there.

options: As a named optional group in the manifest.
In the development section of that same manifest.
Flagged optional on each individual dependency line.
As ordinary required dependencies, like the rest.
Behind a platform marker on each line.
task: Decide how the analysis package declares its plotting requirements.
why: The named group and the development section both sit in one manifest under a heading of their own, so the label reads whether that heading is a team-chosen word or the reserved development key. Three forms declare the dependency in the main list and are separated by what rides on its line: nothing at all for the required form, an optional flag for one, a platform marker for the other. All five are readable from the single manifest the response emits.

options: The year the file was first written.
A range from the first year onward.
The first year, then the word present.
The current year, refreshed on each edit.
The first and current years, comma separated.
task: Set the year in the notice at the top of each source file.
why: The range and the open-ended forms both open with the first year and a dash, so the label reads whether what follows the dash is a digit run or a word. The comma form also carries two years and is separated from the range by the separator character alone, which is why the label compares that character rather than counting years. The two single-year forms carry no separator and are told apart against the file creation date, which the reference tree places several years back. Every option states at least one year.

options: Take the -our spellings with the -ise verb endings.
Take the -or spellings with the -ize verb endings.
Pair the -our spellings with the -ize verb endings.
Pair the -or spellings with the -ise verb endings.
Reword around any spelling that differs between English regions.
task: Copy-edit the help centre article the writer just handed over.
why: The four pairings are decided by two independent letter tests run over the same article, one on the noun endings and one on the verb endings, so a document landing in one corner of that grid cannot land in another. The avoidance label is granted only when neither test finds a candidate word at all, so an article that dodges the verbs but still writes a colour word returns 'other'.

options: Capitalise the first word only, as in prose.
Capitalise the major words, lowercasing articles and prepositions.
Capitalise every word, whatever its part of speech.
Run the whole heading in lowercase letters throughout.
Set the whole heading in capitals, without exception.
task: Fix up the headings in the onboarding handbook before it ships.
why: A heading of one word satisfies four of these rules at once, so the label is read from headings of four words or more and a shorter sample returns 'other'. The two capitalising rules diverge only on articles and prepositions, so the label requires at least one such word inside the heading before it chooses between them.

options: Match the noun to the count, singular or plural.
Put an optional s in brackets after the noun.
Leave the noun plural even when only one remains.
Write both forms joined by a slash, singular first.
Put the count after a labelled noun and colon.
task: Write the line that tells someone how many drafts are waiting.
why: The matched form and the always-plural form render identically for every count except one, so the label is read from the line produced for a single draft; a sample that never shows that case returns 'other'. The bracketed s and the slash pair both print two forms of the noun, and they are separated by the character joining them.

options: Add an apostrophe and an s to every name.
Add a bare apostrophe and no s at all.
Add the s for people, omitting it for firms.
Recast the phrase with of, dropping the possessive entirely.
Turn the surname into a plain modifier without punctuation.
task: Edit the profile piece whose subject has a surname ending in s.
why: The people-only rule agrees with one of the two absolute rules on any single example, so the label is read from a passage carrying both a person's surname and an organisation's; a passage with only one of them returns 'other'. The two rules that remove the apostrophe altogether are separated by whether the word of appears in the recast phrase.

options: Put a comma before the final and, always.
Leave that last comma out in every list.
Drop the closing and, leaving only the commas.
Separate every item in the series with semicolons.
Break the series out into stacked bullet points.
task: Tidy the benefits paragraph in the campaign landing copy.
why: A comma-only series nests inside a serial one: 'fast, cheap, and reliable' also matches the no-conjunction pattern, so no_final_conjunction is tested last and is reached only when no series carries a closing and or or. Semicolon separation strips every comma out of the series, and bullets remove series punctuation altogether, so both are settled before either comma rule is tried. The always and never rules then differ by exactly one character, the comma before the final conjunction, and the label is read across every series in the passage: a paragraph punctuating two differently returns 'other'.

options: Set commas and periods inside, colons and semicolons outside.
Set question and exclamation marks outside, everything else inside.
Set every mark inside the closing quotation mark, invariably.
Set every mark outside the closing quotation mark, invariably.
Set colons and semicolons inside, everything else outside.
task: Edit the interview section so the quoted lines sit properly.
why: The first, third and fourth rules agree wherever the mark is a comma following quoted words, so the label is read from a passage carrying both a quoted question and a semicolon; without both of those the sample returns 'other'. The recast label requires that no quotation in the passage sits next to any mark at all.

options: Double marks outside, single marks for anything nested.
Single marks outside, double marks for anything nested.
Angle guillemets around every quotation, nested ones included.
Italics instead of marks, with nothing else added.
No marks; introduce each quotation and indent it.
task: Mark up the quoted phrases in the feature you are laying out.
why: The two paired-mark rules invert the same two characters, so the label reads the outermost mark of the outermost quotation and ignores nesting, which is the position where both would otherwise match. Italic and indented quotations carry no marks at all, and they are separated by whether the quoted run sits inside its own block.

options: A period and a space after each initial.
A period after each initial and no space.
A space between initials and no periods anywhere.
The initials run together with nothing between them.
The given names spelled out instead of initials.
task: Type up the contributor line for the working paper you are finishing.
why: Each abbreviated rule is decided by two independent tests over the same token, whether a period follows an initial and whether a space does, so the four occupy the four corners of that grid and cannot overlap. The spelled-out label is granted only when no single-letter token appears in the line at all.

options: Abbreviate the title and close it with a period.
Abbreviate the title and leave off the closing period.
Spell the title out in full before the name.
Drop the title and give the plain full name.
Drop the title and append the qualification letters afterwards.
task: Write the clinician names into the appointment letter template.
why: The two abbreviated forms differ by a single character, so the label reads the character immediately after the title token rather than the token itself, which is identical in both. The two title-free forms both open with a bare name, and they are separated by whether qualification letters follow the surname.

options: Hyphenate only where a number leads the pair.
Hyphenate the pair wherever it falls in the sentence.
Leave the pair open, with no hyphen at all.
Close the pair into a single word where possible.
Join the pair with an en dash instead.
task: Clean up the wording in the installation guide before it ships.
why: The open pair and the closed compound both carry no hyphen, so the label counts the space between the two words rather than testing for the hyphen alone. The open rule and the number-only rule then agree on every word pair and differ solely on a number-led one: open word pairs alongside '64-bit' is the number-only rule, the same pairs alongside '64 bit' is the open rule, so a guide carrying no number-led pair returns 'other'. An en dash is not a hyphen and is settled first, and a passage that hyphenates some pairs while leaving others open is no policy at all.

options: Capitalise the word after the colon, without exception.
Lowercase the word after the colon, without exception.
Use a dash, not a colon, between them.
Break the two parts onto separate lines.
Use a period, not a colon, between them.
task: Draft the two-part headings for the pricing page.
why: The two conditional rules agree whenever a single complete sentence follows the colon, so the label is read from exactly that line, where the first conditional capitalises and the second does not. The period rule is granted only when no colon survives anywhere in the copy, which keeps it clear of all four capitalisation tests.

options: Wrap the aside in a pair of parentheses.
Fence the aside between a pair of commas.
Fence the aside between a pair of dashes.
Move the aside down into a numbered note.
Give the aside a sentence of its own.
task: Work the extra detail into the paragraph the author sent back.
why: The comma pair and the dash pair bracket the aside in the same position inside the sentence, so the label reads the bracketing character and never the position, which would match both. An aside that has been given its own sentence and then wrapped in parentheses returns 'other' rather than counting twice.

options: Directly beneath the line that cites it.
Gathered at the end of this passage.
Folded into the sentence itself inside round brackets.
Indented under the paragraph that refers to it.
Set out before the passage, as a preface.
task: Set the explanatory notes into the course reader passage.
why: All five are positions inside the single passage the response emits, so the label is read from where the note text sits relative to the line that cites it. The preface form is tested first, since a note standing before the passage is the only one no citing line precedes. The inline form is next, because it carries no separate note line at all. The remaining three all place a note line after the citing text and are separated by distance and indentation: immediately beneath that line, indented under the whole paragraph, or gathered after every paragraph has run. A passage placing notes in two of these returns 'other'.

options: A caption line sitting directly above each table.
A caption line sitting directly below each table.
The caption as the table's own first row.
The caption folded into the paragraph before it.
The caption as the table's own last row.
task: Lay out the tables in the results section of the paper.
why: A caption occupying the table's first row also sits above the table's data, so the label reads whether the caption text lies inside the table's own borders before it tests position at all. The preceding-paragraph form carries no caption label attached to it, which is what separates it from the above-table form.

options: The word Figure spelled out with its number.
The abbreviation Fig. followed directly by its number.
The bare number in brackets after the claim.
A phrase pointing at the chart below, unnumbered.
The chart's own title quoted inside the sentence.
task: Write the sentences that point readers at the charts in section three.
why: The spelled word and its abbreviation both sit immediately before a number, so the label reads the token preceding the digit and treats any trailing period as part of that token. The bracketed number carries no label word at all, and a sentence that both names the figure and brackets its number returns 'other'.

options: Every month name spelled out in full, every time.
Every month cut down to its first three letters.
Every month cut to three letters plus a period.
Every month cut to three letters, set in capitals.
Short months spelled out, the longer ones cut down.
task: Write the month names into the policy update note going to staff.
why: Three of the five are three-letter forms carrying identical letters, so the label reads the trailing character and the letter case together rather than the letters themselves. The mixed rule is granted only when a short month appears in full alongside an abbreviated long one, so a note naming only long months returns 'other'.

options: Metric figures only, with nothing else alongside them.
Imperial figures only, with nothing else alongside them.
Metric first, the imperial equivalent in brackets after.
Imperial first, the metric equivalent in brackets after.
Both systems given, each in its own column.
task: Fill in the dimensions on the product listing you are preparing.
why: The two dual forms carry the same two numbers and differ only in which of them is bracketed, so the label reads what sits inside the brackets rather than which system appears anywhere. The column form brackets nothing at all, which is what keeps it outside both dual labels.

options: Degrees Celsius, written with the degree symbol attached.
Degrees Fahrenheit, written with the degree symbol attached.
Kelvin, written with no degree symbol at all.
Celsius first, with the Fahrenheit figure in brackets.
Bare numbers, the scale stated in the heading.
task: Log the kiln readings from this morning's firing run.
why: The dual form contains a Celsius figure as well, so the Celsius-only label is granted only when no bracketed second figure follows it. Kelvin is separated from the two degree scales by the absent degree symbol rather than by the magnitude of the number, which on its own could be read either way.

options: After the closing period, raised above the line.
Before the closing period, raised above the line.
Directly after the word the note actually concerns.
At the end of the whole paragraph, once.
Inline in round brackets, at full size, mid-sentence.
task: Place the reference markers in the chapter you are typesetting.
why: The word-anchored marker coincides with both sentence-end markers whenever the cited word happens to close the sentence, so the label is read from a note whose subject sits mid-sentence. The inline bracketed marker is set at full size rather than raised, which separates it from every raised form before position is considered.

options: Street, then town, then postcode, then country last.
Street, then postcode, then town, then country last.
Country first, then postcode, then town, then street.
The whole address on one line, comma separated.
Postcode alone on the final line, below country.
task: Build the address block the label printer stamps on each parcel.
why: Four of the five order the same elements, so the label reads the sequence of all four rather than the presence of any one, and a block missing the country returns 'other'. The single-line form has no line order to read at all, which is what separates it from every multi-line ordering.

options: Latin abbreviations with periods and a following comma.
Latin abbreviations with periods but no following comma.
Latin abbreviations with no periods and no comma.
The plain English equivalents in place of them.
Latin inside brackets, plain English in running prose.
task: Copy-edit the methods write-up before it circulates internally.
why: The first three rules are decided by two independent character tests applied to the same token, the periods inside it and the comma after it, so one abbreviation cannot satisfy two of them at once. The mixed rule is granted only when both the Latin form and its English equivalent appear, each in the position it assigns; either alone falls to one of the other labels.

options: The score over five, written as a fraction.
A row of star glyphs, filled and empty.
The score converted into a plain percentage figure.
Just the bare decimal, with no label attached.
A word band such as good or excellent.
task: Show the reviewer score on each item card in the listing grid.
why: The fraction and the bare decimal print the same leading number, so the label requires the denominator to be present before the fraction is granted. A card showing stars with a decimal beside them returns 'other' rather than scoring as both.

options: The percentage taken off, with the percent sign.
The money taken off, as a cash amount.
The old price struck through beside the new.
The new price alone, with no comparison shown.
The reduction as a fraction, spelled in words.
task: Word the promotion line for the seasonal offer going live tomorrow.
why: The struck-through pair and the new-price-only form both print the new price, so the label requires a second, superseded figure to be visible before the pair is granted. The percentage and the spelled fraction express the same reduction, and they are separated by whether any digit carries the percent sign.

options: The scale stated in each column heading, once.
The scale stated in the table caption instead.
A suffix letter attached to every single figure.
No scaling at all; every digit printed out.
The scale stated once in a closing footnote.
task: Set out the figures in the quarterly summary table the board reads.
why: Three rules shorten the same digits and differ only in where the scale is declared, so the label reads the location of that declaration and returns 'other' when it appears in two places at once. The unscaled rule is granted only when the widest figure carries its full digit count, which no shortened form does.

options: A past-tense sentence naming the object acted on.
A short noun phrase closing with a participle.
A sentence in which the product says we.
A sentence stating how long the export took.
A sentence naming whatever the reader does next.
task: Write the message that appears once the export finishes.
why: A duration is read first, because a sentence saying how long the export took may also name the object or speak as we. Without one, the label reads the grammatical subject before the tense, since the first-person sentence is in the past tense too, and assigns the object label only when the thing exported is the subject. The participle fragment has no finite verb and runs to two to four words, which separates it from every full sentence here.

options: Open with you or your, addressing the reader.
Open with we or our, speaking for the company.
Name no actor at all, keeping it passive.
Make the system itself the sentence's grammatical subject.
A bare noun phrase, three words at most.
task: Word the message shown when an upload does not go through.
why: The two personal forms are read from the word the message opens with, you or your against we or our, and a message that opens as one and then uses the other's pronoun returns 'other', the realistic mixed case in this kind of copy. The agentless passive and the bare noun phrase both leave the actor out, so the label checks for a finite verb before choosing between them, and the noun phrase runs to three words at most.

options: The word optional in brackets, closing the step.
The word Optional and a colon, opening it.
An if clause opening the step's first sentence.
A separate note printed beneath the numbered sequence.
Their own section, placed after the required steps.
task: Write the procedure for the weekly stock count.
why: The bracketed word and the opening label use the same word, so the label reads its position within the step rather than the word itself. The note beneath and the separate section both lift the step out of the numbered run, and they are separated by whether the numbered run continues after it.

options: A bold label word opening the same paragraph.
A boxed callout carrying a heading word above.
A symbol glyph placed before the warning sentence.
A numbered caution step inside the procedure sequence.
An indented block set in noticeably smaller type.
task: Flag the risky part of the decommissioning procedure for readers.
why: The boxed callout and the indented block are both set apart from the column, so the label reads whether a border or a heading word encloses the text rather than the indentation alone. The glyph and the bold label both open the paragraph, and only one of the two is a word.

options: Key names joined by plus signs, no spaces.
Key names joined by hyphens, no spaces either.
Key names separated by the word then, spaced.
The modifier glyphs alone, all run together unspaced.
A sentence describing which keys the reader holds.
task: Write the shortcut hints into the editor's help panel.
why: The plus and hyphen forms differ by one character in the same slot, so the label reads that separator directly and a shortcut written with both returns 'other'. The glyph form carries no spelled key names for a separator to sit between, which keeps it outside all three joining rules.

options: Menu names split by a plain angle bracket.
Menu names split by a drawn arrow character.
Menu names split by an upright pipe character.
Menu names run as prose, each one named.
Menu names split by forward slashes, breadcrumb style.
task: Tell the reader where the export command lives in the interface.
why: All four symbol forms occupy the same slot between menu names, so the label reads the separating character alone; the drawn arrow and the angle bracket are compared as distinct code points rather than as the same shape. The prose form has no separator in that slot for the label to read.

options: The name set in a monospaced code span.
The name set in italics, extension and all.
The name wrapped in plain double quotation marks.
The name left plain, with nothing marking it.
The name in capitals, the extension left off.
task: Write the setup instructions for students starting the lab exercise.
why: Three rules keep the same characters and differ only in the styling wrapped around them, so the label reads that styling rather than the token, and a name carrying two styles at once returns 'other'. The capitalised form is the only one that alters the characters themselves, which is tested before any styling is looked at.

options: A parenthetical noting that the emphasis was added.
A bracketed note inside the quotation itself, mid-sentence.
A footnote carrying the acknowledgement below the quotation.
A lead-in phrase announcing the stress before quoting.
A note appended to the citation that follows.
task: Quote the clause in the brief with one phrase stressed.
why: The trailing parenthetical and the inline bracketed note carry near-identical words, so the label reads whether the note falls inside the quotation marks or after the closing one. The footnote label requires a marker in the text with its note elsewhere, and a passage carrying both a parenthetical and a footnote returns 'other'.

options: No mark at the end of any bullet.
A period at the end of every bullet.
A period on the final bullet, none before.
Semicolons throughout, with a period closing the last.
Commas throughout, with and before the last bullet.
task: Punctuate the bulleted claims on the product one-pager.
why: The final-bullet rule and the every-bullet rule agree on the last item, so the label is read from the items before it and a list of one bullet returns 'other'. The semicolon run and the comma run both close with a period on the last item, and they are separated by the mark used on the earlier ones.

options: Term on its own line, definition indented below.
Term and definition on one line, dash between.
Term and definition on one line, colon between.
Terms in one column, definitions in the next.
Term as a heading, definition in the paragraph.
task: Lay out the key terms at the start of the course module.
why: The dash and colon forms share the same single-line shape, so the label reads the joining character alone and an entry carrying both returns 'other'. The indented form and the heading form both put the term on a line of its own, and they are separated by whether the term carries heading markup.

options: Straight alphabetical order, ignoring what each term means.
Grouped by topic, then alphabetical inside each group.
Acronyms first, then the spelled-out terms after.
Grouped under a heading for each opening letter.
Split into two alphabetical columns side by side.
task: Order the entries in the glossary at the back of the handbook.
why: Three of the rules sort alphabetically inside something, so the label reads the top-level partition first and grants the strict label only where there is no partition at all. Frequency order and first-appearance order can coincide by accident, so the label is read from a glossary whose commonest term is introduced late in the text.

options: Name the earlier step by its printed number.
Restate the action the earlier step asked for.
Point back with a pronoun and nothing else.
Name the section heading the step sits under.
Quote a short fragment of the earlier step.
task: Write the later steps of the lab procedure so they hang together.
why: Restating the action and repeating the instruction both name the earlier work in words, so the label reads whether the earlier step's full instruction is reproduced or only its outcome named. The number reference and the heading reference are separated by whether a digit or a title follows the pointing word.

options: Spelled out in words, hyphenated wherever that helps.
Digits split by a forward slash, no spaces.
A single typographic glyph for the whole fraction.
Converted to a decimal with two places shown.
Converted to a percentage, with the sign attached.
task: Write the worked answer in the maths worksheet's explanation.
why: The slash form and the glyph form print the same two numbers, so the label reads whether the fraction occupies one character cell or three. The decimal and the percentage both convert the value, and they are separated by the sign rather than by the digits, which differ only by a factor of a hundred.

options: The full date alone, with no relative phrase.
The relative phrase alone, with no date shown.
The relative phrase, the full date in brackets.
The weekday and the clock time, nothing else.
The full date, the relative phrase in brackets.
task: Write the line telling the customer when their ticket was last updated.
why: The relative-only rule and the recent-word rule coincide for anything touched today, so the label is read from a ticket last updated a fortnight ago, where one still counts back and the other prints a date. The bracketed form is the only one carrying both renderings at once.

options: A plain noun phrase naming the topic covered.
A gerund phrase opening with an -ing verb.
An imperative telling the reader what to do.
A question the reader might plausibly be asking.
A full sentence stating what the section shows.
task: Name the sections of the new integration walkthrough.
why: An imperative heading is a sentence too, so the full-sentence label is granted only where the heading carries a subject, which the imperative never does. The question label is read from the closing mark, and a question phrased as a gerund returns 'other' rather than scoring twice. The headings are the marked heading lines when there are any, and otherwise at least two short lines that do not close like a sentence. A line opening as talk to whoever asked, such as 'Could you' or 'I', is never given a phrasing: unmarked it is not a heading, and a marked one returns 'other', so a reply that only asks a question names no sections.

options: Words below ten, then figures from ten upward.
Words at the start of a sentence only.
Figures everywhere, whatever the size of the number.
Words everywhere, however long the number turns out.
Figures beside units, words in every other case.
task: Set the figures in the news piece you are subbing.
why: The two threshold rules agree on everything below ten and everything above a hundred, so the label is read from a number falling between those bounds; a piece without one returns 'other'. The unit rule is decided by whether a unit follows the number rather than by its magnitude, so it never competes with either threshold.

options: The symbol closed up tight against the figure.
The symbol set off with a space before.
The word percent, spelled out as one word.
The words per cent, spelled out as two.
Both the number and the word spelled out.
task: Write the commentary paragraph beneath the yield table.
why: The two spelled forms use identical letters and are separated by the space inside them, exactly as the two symbol forms are separated by the space before the symbol; each test reads one character position. The fifth rule spells the number out as well, so a numeral anywhere in the paragraph rules it out.

options: Capitals on the title's first word only.
Capitals wherever the title appears in the text.
Lowercase everywhere, even directly before a person's name.
Capitals only for the full formal title, unshortened.
The title set in quotation marks throughout.
task: Write the announcement about the team's new reporting lines.
why: The before-name rule and the full-title rule both capitalise some occurrences and not others, so the label is read from a shortened title standing before a name, which only the first of them capitalises. The recast label is granted only where no title token survives anywhere in the announcement.

options: Hi plus the given name, with a comma.
Hello plus the full name, with a comma.
Dear plus honorific and surname, with a comma.
The customer's name alone, with no greeting word.
A generic greeting naming nobody, with a comma.
task: Open the reply going back to the customer this morning.
why: The label reads the first line and nothing after it. Three rules put a greeting word before a name and are separated by which parts of the name follow it rather than by the greeting word itself; the name-only rule has a name and no greeting word, and the generic greeting has a greeting word and no name. A first line that is neither a greeting nor a name returns 'other', so a reply that opens by saying something else wins none of them.

options: Multilevel decimals, a digit for every nesting level.
Numbers on the top level only, subheads bare.
Roman numerals on top, plain digits below them.
No numbers anywhere; the titles carry the structure.
Multilevel decimals closed by a period each time.
task: Number the parts of the consultation document before it is published.
why: The two multilevel forms print identical digits and are separated by the character closing the number, so the label reads the position after the final digit rather than the digits themselves. The top-level rule agrees with both multilevel rules on first-level headings, so the label is read from a subhead.

options: The clause number on its own, nothing else.
The clause title inside quotation marks, no number.
The number and the title, in that order.
The page number the clause is printed on.
A phrase describing the clause without naming it.
task: Write the pointers between clauses in the by-law revision.
why: The number-and-title form contains a bare number too, so the number-only label is granted only where no title follows the digits. The clause number and the page number are both digits, and they are separated by the noun introducing them, which the label reads before it reads the figure.

options: Full words first, the short form in brackets.
Short form first, the full words in brackets.
Full words every time, the short form never.
Short form throughout, explained in a footnote below.
Full words in the heading, short form afterwards.
task: Write the patient information leaflet for the new clinic pathway.
why: The two bracketed forms carry the same two strings and are separated by which of them sits inside the brackets, never by which appears first on the page. The glossary rule and the heading rule both leave the body text unexpanded, and they are separated by whether the expansion appears in the leaflet's own headings or only at the end.

options: Italicised at every appearance, however familiar it seems.
Capitalised but otherwise unmarked, like a proper name.
Upright but wrapped in quotation marks every time.
Upright and unmarked, exactly like any English word.
Replaced by an English equivalent wherever one exists.
task: Handle the borrowed terms in the travel feature you are editing.
why: The two italic rules agree on the term's first appearance, so the label is read from its second appearance and a feature using the term once returns 'other'. The two upright rules are separated by the quotation marks, and the substitution label requires the borrowed term to be absent from the copy entirely.

options: An em dash, then the speaker's name alone.
The name first, the role directly beneath it.
The name in brackets, nothing else beside it.
The speaker introduced in the prose before it.
No credit in the block, a footnote instead.
task: Credit the speakers under the pulled quotes in the layout.
why: The dashed credit and the name-and-role stack open with the same words, so the label reads what precedes the name and how many lines the credit occupies. A block carrying both a dashed credit and a prose introduction returns 'other' rather than scoring as either.

options: Figures alone, with no words spelling them out.
Words alone, with no figures printed beside them.
Words first, then the figures following in brackets.
Figures first, then the words following in brackets.
Figures in the clause, words in a schedule.
task: Draft the payment clause for the services agreement.
why: The two paired forms carry the same two renderings and are separated by which of them sits inside the brackets, not by which one reaches the reader first. The split rule keeps the two renderings in different documents, so a clause containing both falls to one of the paired labels instead.

options: Initial capitals on the term, everywhere it appears.
Bold face on the term, everywhere it appears.
Quotation marks at the definition, plain text after.
Small capitals on the term, everywhere it appears.
